title: Sort an Array
description:
Given an array of integers `nums`, sort the array in ascending order and return it.

You must solve the problem **without using any built-in sorting functions** in `O(n log n)` worst-case time complexity and with minimal extra space.
hints: A naive Quick Sort degrades to O(n^2) on already-sorted or duplicate-heavy inputs unless carefully randomized and 3-way partitioned.
Merge Sort divides the array into two halves, recursively sorts each half, and merges the two sorted halves in O(n) time, guaranteeing O(n log n) worst-case performance.
Pre-allocate a single temporary buffer of length n and reuse it across merge calls to avoid repeated allocations.

examples.explanation: Sorting [5, 2, 3, 1] in ascending order produces [1, 2, 3, 5].
Duplicate values are preserved in sorted order: [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 5].
Negative values precede zero and positive values in ascending order.

title: Sort Colors
description:
Given an array `nums` with `n` objects colored red, white, or blue, sort them **in-place** so that objects of the same color are adjacent, with the colors in the order red, white, and blue.

We use the integers `0`, `1`, and `2` to represent the color red, white, and blue, respectively.

You must solve this problem without using the library's sort function. Can you come up with a one-pass algorithm using only `O(1)` extra space?
hints: A two-pass counting sort works easily: count how many 0s, 1s, and 2s appear, then overwrite the array.
For a single-pass O(1)-space solution, apply Dijkstra's Dutch National Flag 3-way partitioning with three pointers: low, mid, and high.
Maintain the invariant: nums[0..low-1] are all 0s, nums[low..mid-1] are all 1s, nums[mid..high] are unexamined, and nums[high+1..n-1] are all 2s.

examples.explanation: All 0s are moved to the front, 1s to the middle, and 2s to the end: [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2].
Sorting [2, 0, 1] in-place yields [0, 1, 2].
A single-element array is already sorted.

title: Merge Intervals
description:
Given an array of `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]`, merge all overlapping intervals, and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals in the input.

Two intervals `[a, b]` and `[c, d]` are considered overlapping if they share at least one point (i.e., `max(a, c) <= min(b, d)`). In particular, intervals touching at a single endpoint such as `[1, 4]` and `[4, 5]` must be merged into `[1, 5]`.
hints: If you sort the intervals by their start value in ascending order, any set of overlapping intervals becomes contiguous in the sorted order.
Maintain the last merged interval in your result list. For each next interval [s, e], if s <= last_end, extend last_end = max(last_end, e).
Otherwise, the new interval is disjoint from all previous ones, so append [s, e] to the result.

examples.explanation: Since intervals [1, 3] and [2, 6] overlap, merge them into [1, 6]. [8, 10] and [15, 18] remain separate.
Intervals [1, 4] and [4, 5] touch at endpoint 4 and are considered overlapping, merging into [1, 5].
Sorting first brings [1, 4] before [2, 3]; since [2, 3] lies completely inside [1, 4], the merged result is [[1, 4]].

title: Insert Interval
description:
You are given an array of non-overlapping intervals `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]` represent the start and the end of the `i`-th interval and `intervals` is sorted in ascending order by `start_i`. You are also given an interval `newInterval = [start, end]` that represents the start and end of another interval.

Insert `newInterval` into `intervals` such that `intervals` is still sorted in ascending order by `start_i` and `intervals` still does not have any overlapping intervals (merge overlapping intervals if necessary; intervals sharing an endpoint are considered overlapping).

Return `intervals` after the insertion.
constraints: intervals is sorted by start_i in ascending order and contains no overlapping intervals.
hints: Since intervals is already sorted and non-overlapping, you do not need to re-sort; a single O(n) pass suffices.
Split the pass into three phases: (1) all intervals ending strictly before newInterval[0], (2) all intervals overlapping newInterval (starting <= newInterval[1]), and (3) all remaining intervals.
In phase (2), expand newInterval to [min(newStart, s), max(newEnd, e)] before adding it once to the result.

examples.explanation: [2, 5] overlaps with [1, 3], merging into [1, 5], followed by [6, 9].
[4, 8] overlaps with [3, 5], [6, 7], and [8, 10], merging all four into [3, 10].
Inserting into an empty interval list returns [[5, 7]].

title: Meeting Rooms II
description:
Given an array of meeting time intervals `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]`, return the minimum number of conference rooms required so that all meetings can take place.

A room vacated at time `t` can be immediately reused by another meeting starting at time `t` (i.e., intervals `[a, b]` and `[b, c]` do not overlap).
hints: Sort the meetings chronologically by start time so you allocate rooms in the order meetings begin.
Keep a min-heap storing the end times of all currently active meetings. The top of the heap is the room that frees up earliest.
When a new meeting starts at time s, if the earliest end time in the heap is <= s, pop it (reuse that room), then push the new meeting's end time.

examples.explanation: Meeting [0, 30] overlaps with [5, 10] and [15, 20], while [5, 10] and [15, 20] can share a room; 2 rooms are needed.
[2, 4] finishes before [7, 10] begins, so 1 room suffices.
Back-to-back meetings [1, 5], [5, 10], and [10, 15] touch at endpoints and can all reuse a single room.

title: Largest Number
description:
Given a list of non-negative integers `nums`, arrange them such that they form the largest number and return it as a string.

Since the result may be very large, return a string instead of an integer. The returned string must not contain unnecessary leading zeros (for example, if `nums` contains only zeros such as `[0, 0]`, return `"0"`).
hints: Standard lexicographical string comparison fails on pairs like "3" and "30": "30" > "3", yet "330" > "303".
Compare two stringified numbers a and b by comparing the concatenations (a + b) and (b + a): a should come before b if (a + b) > (b + a).
Handle the all-zeros edge case: after sorting, if the largest element is "0", the entire answer is simply "0".

examples.explanation: Arranging as "2" followed by "10" forms "210", which is greater than "102".
Ordering as ["9", "5", "34", "3", "30"] yields the largest possible number "9534330".
Multiple zeros collapse to a single "0" rather than "00".

title: Wiggle Sort II
description:
Given an integer array `nums`, reorder it **in-place** such that:

`nums[0] < nums[1] > nums[2] < nums[3] ...`

Note that all inequalities are **strict** (`<` at even indices, `>` at odd indices). You may assume the input array always has a valid answer. If multiple valid orderings exist, any valid permutation is accepted.

Can you do it in `O(n)` average time and `O(1)` extra space? The judge validates that the modified `nums` is a permutation of the original array and satisfies the strict wiggle property (`true`).
constraints: It is guaranteed that there will be a valid answer for the given input nums.
hints: An O(n log n) approach sorts a copy of nums, splits it into a smaller half and a larger half, and places each half in reverse order into even and odd positions so equal medians stay as far apart as possible.
To reach O(n) average time, find the median element using 3-way Quickselect instead of full sorting.

Combine 3-way Dutch National Flag partitioning around the median with virtual index mapping idx(i) = (1 + 2 * i) % (n | 1) to place elements > median into odd slots and elements < median into even slots in-place.

examples.explanation: A valid wiggle ordering such as [1, 6, 1, 5, 1, 4] satisfies 1 < 6 > 1 < 5 > 1 < 4.
A valid wiggle ordering such as [2, 3, 1, 3, 1, 2] satisfies 2 < 3 > 1 < 3 > 1 < 2.
Even with adjacent duplicates in the input, [5, 6, 4, 5] separates the two 5s and satisfies 5 < 6 > 4 < 5.

title: Custom Sort String
description:
You are given two strings `order` and `s`. All the characters of `order` are **unique** and were sorted in some custom order previously.

Permute the characters of `s` so that they match the order that `order` was sorted. More specifically, if a character `x` occurs before a character `y` in `order`, then every occurrence of `x` should occur before every occurrence of `y` in the permuted string.

Characters in `s` that do not appear in `order` can be placed at any position. Return **any** permutation of `s` that satisfies this property. The judge validates that your returned string is a permutation of `s` and respects the relative order defined by `order` (`true`).
constraints: order and s consist of lowercase English letters.
All the characters of order are unique.
hints: You can sort the characters of s using a custom comparator that maps each character in order to its index (and unranked characters to 26).
For an even faster O(n + m) solution, count the frequency of each character in s using an array of size 26.
Iterate through order and append each character as many times as it appears in s, then append all remaining characters that were not in order.

examples.explanation: Characters 'c', 'b', and 'a' appear in order as c -> b -> a, so "cbad" (or "dcba", "cdba", etc.) is valid.
'b', 'c', and 'a' must appear in that relative order; 'd' is not in order and can go anywhere, e.g. "bcad".
Following order "kqep", the permutation "kqeep" places 'k', 'q', both 'e's, then 'p'.

title: Pancake Sorting
description:
Given an array of integers `arr` that is a permutation of `[1, 2, ..., arr.length]`, sort `arr` by performing a series of **pancake flips**.

In one pancake flip you do the following steps:
- Choose an integer `k` where `1 <= k <= arr.length`.
- Reverse the sub-array `arr[0...k-1]` (0-indexed).

Return an array of the `k`-values corresponding to a sequence of pancake flips that sort `arr` in ascending order. Any valid answer that sorts the array within `10 * arr.length` flips will be judged as correct. The judge simulates your flip sequence and validates that `arr` ends up sorted within the flip budget (`true`).
constraints: All integers in arr are unique (arr is a permutation of [1, 2, ..., arr.length]).
hints: Think like Selection Sort: place the largest unsorted element into its final position at the end of the unsorted prefix, one element at a time.
To move value x from index idx to its target position (x - 1), first flip the prefix of length (idx + 1) to bring x to index 0, then flip the prefix of length x to move x to index (x - 1).
Each element needs at most 2 flips, so the total number of flips is at most 2 * (n - 1), well under the 10 * n limit.

examples.explanation: The array [1, 2, 3] is already sorted, so an empty list [] of flips is valid.
Flipping prefix k = 2 reverses [2, 1] into [1, 2].

title: Maximum Gap
description:
Given an integer array `nums`, return the maximum difference between two successive elements in its sorted form. If the array contains fewer than two elements, return `0`.

You must write an algorithm that runs in linear time `O(n)` and uses linear extra space `O(n)`.
hints: Comparison-based sorting takes O(n log n) time; to achieve O(n), exploit the Pigeonhole Principle via bucket partitioning (or Radix Sort).
With min value mn and max value mx over n elements, the maximum gap is at least ceil((mx - mn) / (n - 1)).

If each bucket has width b = max(1, (mx - mn) // (n - 1)), no two elements inside the same bucket can form the maximum gap—so you only need to track the minimum and maximum of each bucket and compare consecutive non-empty buckets.

examples.explanation: The sorted form of the array is [1, 3, 6, 9]; either (3, 6) or (6, 9) has the maximum difference of 3.
The array contains fewer than 2 elements, so return 0.
With only two elements 1 and 10000000, the successive difference is 9999999.

title: H-Index
description:
Given an array of integers `citations` where `citations[i]` is the number of citations a researcher received for their `i`-th paper, return the researcher's **h-index**.

According to the definition of h-index: the h-index is the maximum value of `h` such that the given researcher has published at least `h` papers that have each been cited at least `h` times.
hints: A researcher with n papers can have an h-index of at most n, so any citation count greater than n can be capped at n.
Create a frequency array buckets of length n + 1 where buckets[c] counts how many papers have min(citations[i], n) == c.
Scan h from n down to 0 while accumulating the running count of papers with at least h citations; the first h with count >= h is the answer.

examples.explanation: The researcher has 5 papers with citations [3, 0, 6, 1, 5]. Since 3 papers have at least 3 citations each (3, 6, 5), the h-index is 3.
Only 1 paper has at least 2 citations (3), whereas 3 papers have at least 1 citation, so the h-index is 1.
No paper has been cited, so the h-index is 0.
